title: Australia’s opening to break its Indonesia investment drought
gist: Australian investment into Southeast Asia has fallen since 2022 to $104 billion — less than half what Australia puts into New Zealand, with three quarters of it parked in Singapore — and Indonesia holds a mere $7 billion despite being projected as the world's fourth-largest economy by 2050. With Indonesian markets deteriorating under Prabowo (foreign flows down ~7%, rupiah down a record 11%, frontier-market downgrade risk), the argued fix is not more demand-side ambition but government funding of early-stage project preparation to build a pipeline of bankable deals.

insights.claim: Australian investment into Southeast Asia has been going backwards since 2022, falling to $104 billion — less than half of what Australia invests in New Zealand.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
insights.so_what: The stated Australian pivot to Southeast Asia is not showing up in capital flows; treat official regional-engagement rhetoric as a poor predictor of allocation.
insights.quote: the total is less than half of what Australia invests in New Zealand
insights.locator: Australia’s investment into Southeast Asia is going backwards

insights.claim: Three quarters of Australia's Southeast Asia investment goes to Singapore alone, so the regional exposure is far less diversified than the headline number suggests even allowing for Singapore's gateway function.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
insights.so_what: Concentration in one financial hub means Australian capital carries little real exposure to ASEAN growth economies — a gap for anyone selling the region's demographics.
insights.quote: Three quarters of Australia’s investment in Southeast Asia goes to Singapore alone

insights.claim: Total ASEAN–Australia trade is up around $20 billion since 2022 from a base of $178 billion, far short of the trajectory needed to meet the official goal of tripling trade by 2040.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
entities: Invested: Australia’s Southeast Asia Economic Strategy to 2040
insights.so_what: About 11% growth in four years against a target implying roughly 200% by 2040 — the strategy is materially off-pace and likely to attract policy escalation.
insights.quote: Total ASEAN–Australia trade (Opens in new window) is up around $20 billion since 2022 (off a base of $178 billion) – still a long way off the goal of tripling trade by 2040.

insights.claim: Australia's existing regional investment tools include a $2 billion Southeast Asia Infrastructure Financing Facility run by Export Finance Australia and Austrade investment deal teams, yet investment has still not begun to increase.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
insights.so_what: De-risking facilities alone have not moved private capital — evidence that the binding constraint sits upstream of financing.
insights.locator: Other measures include a $2 billion Southeast Asia Infrastructure Financing Facility

insights.claim: The premise of Australia's 2040 Southeast Asia strategy is that countries with strong economic links have a stake in each other's prosperity and are therefore more likely to align on regional peace and security.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
insights.so_what: Economic engagement is being justified on security grounds, which means underperformance on investment carries strategic, not just commercial, consequences for Canberra.
insights.locator: The reasonable theory is that countries who share strong economic links

insights.claim: Australia has only about $7 billion invested in Indonesia, a country with a population pushing 300 million and projected to become the world's fourth-largest economy by 2050.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
insights.so_what: One of the largest gaps between demographic opportunity and actual allocation in the region — the size of the mispricing if governance risk ever normalises.
insights.quote: Australia has a measly $7 billion invested.
insights.locator: Indonesia is perhaps the most instructive case study

insights.claim: Unpredictable regulatory and legal regimes plus pervasive corruption keep Indonesia off-limits for Australian institutional investors, who combine low risk appetites, high fiduciary standards and limited Indonesia literacy.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
insights.so_what: Fiduciary constraints, not returns, are the gating factor — meaning policy must change the evidence base available to trustees, not just the incentives.
insights.locator: Indonesia has long been a tricky market

insights.claim: The delegation of Australian super fund executives that flew to Jakarta after Anthony Albanese's 2022 visit has seemingly not produced a single new major investment.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
insights.so_what: High-profile trade missions are a near-zero-signal event for actual capital deployment; discount them entirely when tracking flows.
insights.quote: has seemingly not yet led to a single new major investment
insights.locator: The delegation of Australian super fund executives

insights.claim: Net foreign flows into Indonesian stocks and government bonds are down around 7% since Prabowo Subianto's election in February 2024, and the rupiah has sunk a record 11% against the US dollar over the same period.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
insights.so_what: Hard evidence of sustained foreign de-risking from Indonesian assets under the current administration — a currency and portfolio-flow trend, not a one-off shock.
insights.quote: the rupiah has sunk a record 11% against the US dollar over the same period
insights.locator: Net foreign flows into Indonesian stocks and government bonds

insights.claim: Indonesia is at serious risk of being downgraded by ratings agencies from an 'emerging' to a 'frontier' market.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
insights.so_what: An index reclassification would force mechanical selling by EM-benchmarked funds — a large, dateable flow risk for Indonesian equities and bonds.
insights.quote: from “emerging” to “frontier” market by ratings agencies
insights.locator: Indonesia is at serious risk of a downgrade

insights.claim: Indonesia's investment climate under Prabowo Subianto has deteriorated from a little cloudy to brewing with storms.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
insights.so_what: Directional call on Indonesian political-economic risk from a regional analyst — bias toward further deterioration rather than mean reversion.
insights.quote: have gone from a little cloudy to brewing with storms
insights.locator: Added to this, Indonesia’s investment skies

themes.theme: Pipeline, not incentives, as the binding constraint

insights.claim: The gap between what the Australian government wants from Southeast Asia investment and what investors actually want is widening, and Canberra can do little to improve the fundamental attractiveness of difficult markets.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
insights.so_what: State ambition cannot override country risk — expect continued underdelivery on regional economic strategies regardless of new facilities announced.
insights.quote: The gap between what the Australian government wants and what investors want is only widening.
insights.locator: The gap between what the Australian government wants

insights.claim: Credible Southeast Asian projects miss out on investment simply because investor caution combined with local skill gaps leaves them not strong on paper, making project preparation rather than capital availability the binding constraint.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
insights.so_what: Reframes the regional infrastructure gap as a documentation and feasibility problem — the cheapest possible intervention point, and an underused one.
insights.quote: Investor caution combined with local skill gaps can mean credible projects miss out on investment simply because they aren’t strong on paper.
insights.locator: Investor caution combined with local skill gaps

insights.claim: Increasing government support for early-stage project preparation and advisory work to grow the pipeline of bankable regional projects is a 2040-strategy recommendation on which there has been no discernible public progress.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
entities: Invested: Australia’s Southeast Asia Economic Strategy to 2040
insights.so_what: A specific, unimplemented policy lever — its activation would be an early signal that Australian capital may finally follow the strategy.
insights.locator: One recommendation, buried in the 2040 strategy

insights.claim: Macquarie has advised that government assistance to Southeast Asian investment would be most productively directed at early-stage project preparation and advisory work.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
insights.so_what: The region's most sophisticated infrastructure investor is pointing at the same bottleneck — corroboration from a party with skin in the game.
insights.quote: Big players like Macquarie have advised (Opens in new window) this is where government assistance would be most productively directed.
insights.locator: Big players like Macquarie have advised

insights.claim: Existing vehicles that could be repurposed for project preparation include DFAT's Partnerships for Infrastructure (P4I) program and KINETIK, a $600 million program supporting sustainable infrastructure investment in Indonesia.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
entities: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
insights.so_what: Named, funded programs that could be redirected without new appropriations — the lowest-friction path to actual deal flow in Indonesia.
insights.locator: expanding existing Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade programs

insights.claim: Government could extend grant funding to project preparation and advisory firms to cover the up-front cost of feasibility studies, with those firms taking a clip of successful investments in the project later.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
insights.so_what: A success-fee-linked public subsidy model for feasibility work — creates a new revenue line for advisory firms operating in ASEAN infrastructure.

insights.claim: Government plays an important countercyclical role by stepping up with funding and practical support to keep economic wheels turning when private sector investment is languishing.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
insights.so_what: Justifies expanded state involvement precisely when country risk is highest — expect more public capital in Indonesian projects as private flows retreat.
insights.locator: Government plays an important countercyclical role

insights.claim: The project-preparation mechanism would mainly yield relatively smaller deals, so its payoff is cumulative rather than transformational.
insights.speaker: Iona Main
insights.so_what: Do not expect a step-change in Australia–Indonesia investment figures; the realistic path is slow accretion over many small transactions.
insights.quote: as the Indonesians say, “sedikit sedikit lama-lama menjadi bukit” – little efforts over time can become a big hill
insights.locator: While this mechanism is likely to yield relatively smaller projects
